blocks.h: Why do parities flip on the right?
p: Removing the element at `i` shifts every later element one position left, so an element that was at an odd index lands at an even index and vice versa. Elements to the left keep their positions. Prefix sums by parity and suffix sums by parity therefore combine with swapped roles.

1664.takeaway: Ways to make fair: track left parity prefix sums and right parity totals; deleting index i swaps the roles of right even/odd sums.

Distances to the `i` smaller elements: `i × x` minus their sum (the array is sorted, so all differences are non-negative and no `abs` is needed)
Sum of differences to the left
Distances to the elements after `i`: their sum minus `x` times their count
Sum of differences to the right

p: `nums = [2,3,5]` (sorted):

For a sorted array, every element to the left is ≤ `x` and every element to the right is ≥ `x`. So `|x − y|` is `x − y` on the left and `y − x` on the right, which turns the sum into counts times `x` minus or plus a prefix/suffix sum, with no absolute values.

1685.takeaway: Sum of absolute differences in a sorted array: split into left and right of each element and use a running prefix sum with the total.

p: `n = 3` (length 5). The search tries 3 first at every position and backs out only when stuck; the first moves:
The first complete sequence found is `[3,1,2,3,2]`, which is the lexicographically largest because larger numbers were tried first at each position.

blocks.h: Why does trying large numbers first give the lexicographically largest answer?
p: Lexicographic order is decided by the earliest differing position. Placing the largest feasible number at the leftmost free position (and exploring in that order, returning on the first success) means no later branch could have a larger value earlier.

bullets: Time: exponential in the worst case, but pruning makes it fast for n ≤ 20 in practice.

1718.takeaway: Lexicographically largest distanced sequence: backtracking left to right trying the largest number first, placing its two copies v apart.

p: When the first characters are equal (as in `cab…` vs `cac…`), choosing blindly could put a smaller continuation first. Comparing the whole remaining strings looks ahead to the first position where they differ and picks the side that will give the larger character there.

p: `nums = [9]`, `maxOperations = 2`:

A bag of 9 split into parts of size at most 3 needs 3 parts, i.e. 2 cuts: `(9 − 1) // 3 = 2`. `9 // 3 = 3` would count the pieces, one too many. The formula `ceil(x/mid) − 1` equals `(x − 1) // mid` for positive integers.

1760.takeaway: Minimum limit of balls: binary search the penalty; a penalty is feasible if the total cuts `(x−1)//mid` fit within the allowed operations.

blocks.h: Why O(26) per substring is acceptable
p: There are O(n²) substrings and each costs 26 steps to scan the count array, so the total is O(26 · n²) ≈ O(n²). With n ≤ 500 that is about 6.5 million operations. Because each substring extends the previous one by one character, the counts never need rebuilding.

p: The string has no leading zeros, so it starts with `1`.

blocks.h: Why does `01` detect a second segment?
p: The string starts with `1` (no leading zeros). A second segment of ones can only begin after a run of zeros, and the point where it begins is a `0` followed by `1`. Conversely, if `01` never appears, once the first block of ones ends only zeros follow.

1784.takeaway: At most one segment of ones in a string starting with 1: it must not contain the substring '01'.

No mismatches: already equal (zero swaps is allowed: 'at most one')
Exactly two mismatches whose letters are crossed: `(a, b)` and `(b, a)`; swapping those two positions in ONE string fixes both
Reverse a tuple to swap its two entries

p: A single swap inside one string exchanges two of its letters. For the strings to become equal, the two mismatched positions must contain the same two letters in opposite order: `s1` has `(a, b)` and `s2` has `(b, a)`. One mismatch can never be fixed (a swap changes two positions), and three or more cannot be fixed by one swap.

bullets: Space: O(1) (at most a few mismatches matter, though the list can grow before the check).

1790.takeaway: One string swap makes strings equal iff there are 0 mismatches, or exactly 2 that are mirror images of each other.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: 0-based index of the winner when there are `i` people
The Josephus recurrence builds the answer for `i` people from the answer for `i − 1`
After the first person is eliminated, the circle of `i − 1` people starts counting from the next person; the winner's index in the old circle is shifted by `k` and wrapped
Shifting the answer back into the bigger circle
One person left: they win, at index 0

p: `n = 5`, `k = 2`: the winner's 0-based index for circles of size 1..5.

With `i` people, person at index `(k − 1) % i` is eliminated, and counting restarts from the person after them. Relabelling the remaining `i − 1` people from 0 gives the smaller game. A position `p` in the smaller game corresponds to position `(p + k) % i` in the larger one. So the answer builds up from 1 person.

1823.takeaway: Josephus problem: iteratively compute the winner's index with pos = (pos + k) % i for circles of growing size.
